A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Selective Attention work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material across appendix reordering and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original language-modeling, HellaSwag, context-pruning, synthetic-task, and ablation results in Section 6 and Appendix A.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds downstream benchmark scores, T5 pre-training results, efficient-attention comparisons, and attention-pattern analyses.

M1.justification: The selection head, masking constraints, shifted cumulative accumulation, greedy context pruning, and memory regularizer are retained. T5 applies the existing mechanism to its decoder without introducing a new component or changing the selective-attention procedure.

E1.justification: Table 1 expands evaluation beyond HellaSwag to ARC Easy and Challenge, CommonSenseQA, OpenBookQA, and PiQA. Appendix A.9 adds T5 span-corruption pre-training. Copy and Parity* already appeared in v1's Figure 1 and Section 2; their new appendix documentation does not establish newly added task coverage.

E2.justification: v2 Appendix A.10 and Figure 7 add evaluated comparisons with H2O, TOVA, Window + 4, and sparse attention. These extend the original dense, additional-head, and local-attention comparisons. Several underlying works were already cited in v1, but these head-to-head results were absent.

E3.justification: Appendix A.9 adds a distinct encoder-decoder experimental setup using T5-small, T5-base, and T5-large, standard span-corruption training, and validation loss per non-padding token after 524,288 steps. This substantially broadens the evaluated model configurations and objective. The original C4 protocols remain unchanged; the added Copy/Parity* settings are newly disclosed details.

E4.justification: Appendix A.11 and Figure 8 add a Variable Assignment case study comparing attention across all three layers with and without selective attention. This extends the earlier selected-layer visualization. The bilinear-form, masking-constraint, self-impact, local-attention, and existing sparsity analyses are retained.

E5.justification: The three-run self-impact averages and two-run sparsity illustration are unchanged. The new T5 table also reports results from three runs, continuing the existing reporting convention. No new uncertainty intervals, significance tests, seed policy, or revised run counts for retained experiments are reported.

E6.justification: v2 adds downstream accuracy results, efficient-attention trade-off curves, and near-zero loss/100% accuracy findings for both methods on Copy and Parity*. Table 7 adds baseline/selective T5 losses of 1.962/1.952, 1.693/1.691, and 1.528/1.522. New downstream results include exceptions: OpenBookQA at d = 20 scores 35.42% versus 35.27%. Original C4 and ablation results are retained; HellaSwag is reported at finer precision.

T1.justification: The attention equations, memory penalty, and pruning reasoning are preserved. Section 4 uses generic task-loss notation instead of explicitly naming perplexity/log-perplexity, without adding a substantive derivation or mathematical result. No new theorem, proof, or formal assumption appears.

C1.justification: The abstract now explicitly claims consistent improvements in downstream-task performance as well as language modeling, broadening the stated scope. The central parameter-free attention contribution, approximately doubled-head equivalence, and 16X/25X/47X memory-saving claims remain.

C2.justification: Appendix A.11 adds a layer-specific interpretation in which value tokens absorb variable identities and later layers identify previous assignments. Appendix A.10 distinguishes post-training pruning methods from methods requiring training. The discussion acknowledges initial encoder-decoder evidence, while Appendix A.9 makes clear that selective attention is applied only to the decoder.

D1.justification: Appendix A.2 newly documents synthetic-task settings: d = 3, batch size 2,048, 65,536 steps, uniformly sampled Copy lengths 1–24, its context construction, and the even-position Parity* loss. Appendix A.9 identifies the T5X code and standard recipe. Figure 2 removes the compiler-optimization caution; the main implementation and hardware disclosures remain.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for ARC, PiQA, CommonSenseQA, OpenBookQA, and T5X. The DCP discussion removes the parameter and auxiliary-loss distinctions and the independent-discovery footnote. The broader positioning around improving attention quality and learning to forget remains substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: Most prose and the main section sequence are preserved. v2 clarifies the masking explanation, edits the abstract and discussion, adds four appendix subsections, reorders the constraint and self-impact ablations, and adds the ICLR publication header. These are localized edits and extensions rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: Table 1 becomes a substantially expanded display covering six benchmark settings with colored outcome highlighting. v2 adds the T5 table and multi-panel Figures 7 and 8 for efficiency comparisons and attention patterns. Figure 4 is relocated and resized; all original figure image content is retained, including renumbered appendix visualizations.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the evidence for the paper's central contribution. Expanded downstream evaluation and T5 experiments test broader applicability, while Figure 7 addresses v1's important lack of direct comparisons with several efficient-attention competitors. The new attention case study also improves mechanistic interpretation. Small gains remain difficult to assess without uncertainty estimates, and the broad consistency claim overlooks ties and OpenBookQA regressions, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial improvement in comparative support.
